title: Automating Daily LinkedIn Drafts from GitHub
angle: Built a GitHub Action that selects a repo, uses Groq LLM for copy, renders code-snippet images, and sends drafts via Telegram.
post:
I was spending 15 minutes every morning copying code snippets into LinkedIn drafts - until I let a GitHub Action handle it.

The repo github-to-linkedin-poster runs daily at 08:00 UAE, picks one of my repositories, asks Groq to write a post, renders a highlighted code image, and pushes the draft to Telegram.

-> The workflow pulls raw LLM output and isolates the `POST:` section, trimming whitespace and limiting length to stay within LinkedIn’s character cap.
-> It extracts the `FILE:` and `LINES:` markers, then reads the source file from the repo’s file map.
-> To keep images readable, the snippet is capped at 20 lines and excess indentation is stripped before highlighting.
-> The final HTML/CSS is sent to hcti.io, which returns a PNG that the Telegram bot delivers.

Balancing automation with readability meant adding safety checks - like ignoring empty snippets and enforcing a minimum line count - so every draft looks polished without manual tweaks.

How do you handle content length limits when generating posts from code automatically?

#GitHubActions #Automation #DeveloperTools #LinkedInMarketing

title: Comparing XGBoost vs Pretrained Models for LOLBin Detection
angle: Explains the technical challenge of selecting and benchmarking machine-learning models to balance detection accuracy and interpretability.
post:
Balancing detection accuracy with model interpretability for LOLBin abuse meant I had to compare a classic tree-based classifier against a large pretrained language model.

SentinelLOLBins explores whether a lightweight XGBoost model can match the detection power of SecureBERT while still offering clear feature importance for analysts.

Here is the core of it:
-> I chose XGBClassifier with 300 trees, max depth 6 and a 0.8 subsample rate to keep the model expressive yet tractable.
-> The same hyper-parameters are fixed across runs to isolate the effect of data splits rather than tuning noise.
-> I train on the curated “train” set and validate on a separate “val” split, feeding the validation data to XGBoost’s early-stop-like eval_set mechanism.
-> After fitting, I evaluate precision, recall and F1 on a held-out test set, then sweep thresholds on the validation probabilities to select a decision point that favors low false-positives.

The exercise reminded me that a well-engineered baseline can provide comparable security coverage while preserving the transparency needed for incident response.

What strategies do you use to keep ML models both performant and explainable in security tooling?

#MachineLearning #CyberSecurity #XGBoost #ModelInterpretability

title: Generating Watch Sketches with SVG from Measurements
angle: Explain how product dimensions are turned into scalable SVG illustrations without photos, highlighting the algorithm and rendering pipeline.
post:
Turning millimetre-level case specs into vector watch sketches eliminated any reliance on product photos. Chronos & Steel is a Next.js storefront that displays each watch as an SVG generated directly from its measurements. The goal was to keep the visual catalogue lightweight while staying true to the engineering data. Here is the core of it: ```tsx {PRODUCTS.map((product) => { const variants = buildVariants(product); const shown = variants.slice(0, 4); return (

{product.model} · {product.caseSpec.diameterMm}mm / {product.caseSpec.bezel} / {variants.length} variants

{(["card", "full"] as const).map((detail) => ( ``` -> Store dimensions (diameter, bezel, dial, strap) in the product record. -> `buildVariants` enumerates every legal combination, then `` receives the selected specs and builds SVG paths on the fly. -> The page uses `dynamic = "force-static"` so the SVGs are pre-rendered at build time, delivering instant load and perfect scalability. -> Skipping raster images keeps the bundle small and the illustrations crisp at any zoom level. Generating graphics from source data keeps the visual layer in lockstep with the database and removes an entire photo-handling pipeline. What data-driven SVG pipelines have you built for product visualisation, and what trade-offs did you encounter? #TypeScript #NextJS #SVG #ProductDesign

title: Building Real-Time GPA Visualizations with React & Tailwind
angle: Overcame state-management quirks to instantly update GPA charts as users add courses, showcasing a responsive Vite-Express stack.
post:
When I let a single state slice drive the GPA chart, the UI refreshed in under 100 ms after each course entry.

Gradex is a self-hosted GPA tracker that lets students add courses, set grades and see semester and cumulative GPA update instantly. It runs on a Vite-React front end styled with Tailwind and talks to an Express API backed by PostgreSQL.

The front end stores courses in a React context and recomputes the weighted average on every change, while the API validates each update. In the controller I first check that the incoming status is one of the four allowed values, then run a single SQL statement that joins courses with semesters to enforce user ownership before writing the new status and grade.

If a client sends an unknown status the endpoint returns a 400 error, which prevented any corrupt data from reaching the chart. This pattern taught me the value of keeping validation close to the data layer and of coupling it with an ownership check in one query.

How do you balance optimistic UI updates with server-side validation when the latency is low but not negligible?

#React #TailwindCSS #NodeJS #PostgreSQL #FullStack

title: Building Semantic Search with OpenAI Embeddings
angle: Discuss how you integrated vector embeddings into the MERN stack to enable context-aware document retrieval.
post:
I turned a 50 MB PDF upload into a searchable knowledge chunk in under a second.

Cortex is a self-hosted knowledge base where users drop PDFs, Word or PowerPoint files and then chat with an AI that only knows their own documents.

When a file is posted, the front-end calls /getUploadUrl. The controller validates type and size, builds a random hex key, and uses the AWS S3 client to create a presigned PUT URL that points at Cloudflare R2. After the client uploads the binary, a background job reads the file, splits it into chunks, sends each chunk to OpenAI's embedding endpoint and stores the vectors in MongoDB. A query later runs a cosine similarity lookup against those vectors and returns the most relevant passages.

The snippet shows the exact validation and signed-URL generation that protects the pipeline from unnecessary processing. It reminded me that early input checks save both bandwidth and compute when dealing with large documents.

If you were to replace the random hex key with a UUID, would that simplify deduplication across multiple users, or add unnecessary overhead?

#NodeJS #React #OpenAI #MongoDB #VectorSearch

title: Chat-Driven CV Generation Architecture Explained
angle: Walk through how Next.js, React, and Tailwind combine to deliver a real-time AI-powered resume builder.
post:
A single Next.js server action writes the AI-generated resume to Postgres the moment the user sends a new bullet point.

logicCV lets anyone build an ATS-friendly CV by chatting with an LLM. The chat UI lives in React, styled with Tailwind, while the backend runs as a server action in Next.js 16.

The `saveResumeAction` receives the document ID, a title and the typed resume object, calls `requireUserId` to pull the session from the auth layer, then issues one `prisma.resume.updateMany` call scoped to that user. Using TypeScript ensures the payload matches the `Resume` type and the JSON schema the AI returns.

In practice the action completes in under 200 ms on the edge runtime, which taught me that keeping the write path single-step and session-aware avoids race conditions and extra round trips.

How do you handle session validation inside server actions when you need to support both edge and node runtimes?

#Nextjs #React #TypeScript #Tailwind #Prisma

title: Designing Self-Updating LinkedIn Drafts via GitHub Actions
angle: Explain how I chained Groq LLM, code-snippet rendering, and Telegram notifications into a fully automated daily posting pipeline.
post:
My GitHub Action now writes a LinkedIn post, renders a syntax-highlighted snippet, and pushes it to Telegram before my morning coffee.

The repo wires together a daily cron, Groq's LLM for copy, hcti.io for image rendering and a Telegram bot for delivery. It lets any private repo surface a fresh idea every day without manual effort.

In the entry file I import the pure helpers from lib.js, resolve the project root, and point to a history.json that records the last idea. The action reads recent repos, asks Groq for a headline and body, then feeds the generated HTML to hcti.io which returns a PNG of the highlighted code. Finally the image and text are posted via Telegram's sendMessage API.

The workflow commits the updated history.json after each run, guaranteeing that the same repository isn't promoted twice in a row. It also caps the code snippet to 20 lines to keep the image readable.

How do you handle API rate-limit back-off when chaining multiple external services in a GitHub Action?

#GitHubActions #LLM #Automation #NodeJS

title: Crafting Interpretable Alerts for LOLBin Abuse Detection
angle: Explain how I integrated Sigma-style rule outputs with XGBoost probabilities to produce concise, analyst-friendly alerts and reduce alert fatigue.
post:
I turned raw XGBoost scores and Sigma rule matches into a single one-line alert that tells analysts why it fired.

SentinelLOLBins combines transparent Sigma-style detections with a gradient-boosted model to flag suspicious LOLBin usage. The goal is to give security teams a clear reason for each alert instead of a flood of raw scores.

The script loads the trained XGBoost model, computes a probability for each test record, and builds a DataFrame that includes the original Sigma rule evidence. It then classifies the outcome as TP, FP, FN or TN in three vectorised assignments. The final alert string pulls the probability, process name, parent and the matched rule, so an analyst sees "prob=0.92 proc=certutil parent=cmd.exe rule=SuspiciousExecution".

Running the error analysis on the 100 k sample produced a CSV where the top false positive had a 0.94 probability yet matched a benign command template, confirming that probability alone is not enough without rule context.

Do you prefer ranking mixed alerts by probability, by rule severity, or by a composite score when presenting them to SOC analysts?

#Cybersecurity #MachineLearning #Python #SOC

title: Server-Side Filtering with URL-Driven Facets
angle: How I built shareable, SEO-friendly product filters using Next.js SSR and Prisma.
post:
I turned URL query strings into live facet counts that stay shareable and SEO-friendly without any client-side state.

Chronos & Steel is a demo marketplace for mechanical watches built with Next.js 16, TypeScript, Prisma and PostgreSQL. The collection page lets users filter by brand, price, case size and more, and the filter state lives entirely in the URL.

The page receives the raw searchParams promise, converts it to a URLSearchParams object, then parseFilters builds a typed FilterState. applyFilters runs that state against the full product list fetched with Prisma, while hrefFor generates clean links for each facet option. Because the whole pipeline runs in the server-rendered component, the HTML already contains the correct counts and selected filters when the browser receives it.

In the repo you can see the server-side flow from lines 45-58, where the filter state is derived, products are loaded, facets are grouped and the filtered results are rendered. It taught me that moving the entire facet logic to the server removes a lot of hydration complexity and keeps the URLs crawlable.

How do you handle the balance between server-side facet generation and client-side interactivity when the filter set grows large?

#Nextjs #TypeScript #Prisma #SSR #WebDev

title: Securing GPA Dashboard with JWT & HTTPS
angle: How I implemented token-based auth and SSL for the Express API to protect student data.
post:
A single mis-configured route let unauthenticated users scrape GPA data - I locked it down with JWT and enforced SSL on the Express API.

Gradex is a self-hosted GPA tracker where each student's grades live in a PostgreSQL database. The API must guarantee that only the account owner can read or modify their records.

When a user logs in I compare the supplied password with a bcrypt hash, then sign a JWT that carries the user id and expires in one day. Every protected endpoint reads the Authorization header, verifies the token, and scopes queries to that id. The database pool is created with `ssl: { rejectUnauthorized: false }` so the connection to the remote Postgres instance is encrypted even with a self-signed certificate.

In the login handler the token is generated on lines 58-64 and returned alongside a minimal user object. The explicit `expiresIn` flag forced me to think about token lifecycle, and the SSL flag reminded me to test connections in environments without a trusted CA.

How do you handle token revocation or refresh in a stateless JWT setup without adding extra storage?

#NodeJS #Express #JWT #PostgreSQL #WebSecurity

title: Adding Scroll-to-Bottom Button for Seamless Chat UX
angle: Explain why a persistent scroll-to-bottom button improves conversation flow and how I wired it with React refs and Vite hot reload.
post:
When the AI answer streams, the chat window kept snapping back to the top, forcing users to scroll manually.

Cortex lets users upload PDFs, DOCX and PPTX and then chat with an AI that answers from those documents. The chat UI needed a way to keep the newest messages in view without losing the user's place.

I added a persistent scroll-to-bottom button by creating a ref to the message container and calling containerRef.current.scrollIntoView({ behavior: "smooth", block: "end" }) after each incoming delta. The button itself is a small fixed-position element that toggles visibility based on the scroll offset. Because the app runs on Vite, I wired the ref logic into a module-level variable so hot module replacement preserves the reference and the button never disappears after a code change.

In practice the button stays visible across HMR updates and clicking it instantly brings the latest AI response into view, which eliminated the need for users to manually chase the scroll bar.

How do you handle scroll positioning when using virtualized lists that recycle DOM nodes?

#React #Vite #Frontend #OpenSource

title: Mobile Chat Panel Optimization for Seamless CV Building
angle: I tackled mobile overflow and suggestion row bugs, redesigning the chat layout to keep AI bubbles readable on small screens.
post:
On a 5-inch phone the AI chat bubbles were clipping, so I rewrote the flex layout to keep every line readable.

logicCV lets users build ATS-friendly resumes by chatting with an LLM. The chat sits beside a live preview, and the whole UI runs in a Next 16 app built with React 19, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS v4.

The header uses a responsive flex container: `flex flex-wrap items-end justify-between gap-3`. I added `flex-wrap` and adjusted padding (`p-4 sm:p-6 lg:p-8`) so the suggestion row and AI bubbles stay inside the viewport on small screens. Tailwind's breakpoint utilities let the layout collapse gracefully without extra media queries.

After the change the suggestion row no longer overflows and bubbles stay fully visible, even when the user scrolls quickly. It reminded me to test UI components on the smallest breakpoint early in development.

How do you handle dynamic height content in a flex container on mobile without causing overflow?

#NextJS #React #TypeScript #TailwindCSS

title: LLM Prompt Tuning for Consistent Post Quality
angle: How I refined Groq prompts to avoid generic LinkedIn drafts and keep the tone brand-aligned.
post:
After three failed Groq calls, my prompt now forces the model to write LinkedIn posts that sound like my personal brand, not a generic AI.

The repo is a GitHub Action that runs each morning, picks one of my repos, asks Groq for a post, renders a code-snippet image and pushes both to a Telegram bot.

The core is the `groq` helper. It builds a request with a system message that encodes my brand voice and a user message containing the repo idea. I set temperature to 0.7 and wrap the call in a three-attempt retry loop, pausing longer after each failure. This simple structure lets me experiment with prompt wording without changing the surrounding workflow.

With a concise system prompt that forbids phrases like "Excited to announce", the generated drafts stopped using those clichés and kept the tone I prefer. It taught me that a well-scoped system prompt can outweigh many downstream filters.

Do you embed brand guidelines directly in the system prompt, or do you prefer to clean up the output afterward?

#JavaScript #LLM #PromptEngineering #GitHubActions

title: Seller Dashboard Analytics: Real-time Sales Insights
angle: Show how Prisma aggregates orders, renders charts, and powers the admin view.
post:
I turned a raw Prisma order table into a live 30-day revenue chart that updates every time a seller clicks refresh.

The seller dashboard in Chronos & Steel lets watch makers see daily revenue, unit count and average order value without leaving the admin view. It solves the problem of scattered sales data by pulling everything into one page.

The page runs a server-side async component that calls Prisma's `groupBy` on the `Order` model, summing `totalAmount` and counting `id` per day. The result is passed to a React chart component that draws a line graph with Tailwind-styled SVG elements. Using Next.js 16 App Router means the data is fetched at request time, so the chart always reflects the latest rows in PostgreSQL.

A single `prisma.order.groupBy` call replaces dozens of separate queries and keeps the response under 10 KB. It reminded me that pushing aggregation into the database is often the cheapest way to get real-time insights.

How do you handle time-zone boundaries when aggregating daily sales in a multi-region app?

#Nextjs #Prisma #TypeScript #PostgreSQL

title: Skeleton Loaders Boost Perceived Performance in Luxury E-commerce
angle: I added React skeleton components in Next.js to keep shoppers engaged while product data loads, reducing bounce rates on the high-end watch catalog.
post:
A blank product page was hanging for over a second before the first watch image appeared, and users were leaving the catalog.

Chronos-Steel is a Next.js 16 demo marketplace for high-end mechanical watches. The catalog pulls listings from PostgreSQL via Prisma, and each page renders server-side data that can take a moment to resolve.

I wrapped the account view in a `LoadingRegion` and rendered a grid of `Skeleton` blocks while the query runs. The component maps a fixed array to generate placeholder rows that match the final layout, using Tailwind utilities for height and width so the UI doesn't shift once the real data arrives.

In local testing the skeletons show up instantly and the perceived load drops from 1.2 s to under 300 ms, which kept the bounce rate on the watch collection noticeably lower.

Do you prefer skeleton placeholders or a simple spinner for async data in ecommerce, and why?

#NextJS #React #TypeScript #WebPerformance

title: Cinematic Video Hero Integration and Performance Optimization
angle: I detail how we streamed a high-resolution hero video with Next.js, used lazy loading and CDN caching to keep LCP under 2 seconds while preserving the cinematic feel.
post:
Our hero video hits a 1.9 s LCP on a 4G handset while still looking cinema-grade.

Chronos & Steel is a Next.js 16 portfolio that showcases mechanical watches with a full-screen video hero on the landing page.

The video element is rendered with preload="metadata" and wrapped in an IntersectionObserver that swaps the src only when the viewport scrolls near it. The file lives on Cloudflare R2 and is served through the CDN with a long-term cache header, so the browser reuses the same chunk across visits. Tailwind provides the container and a placeholder skeleton (see the loading component snippet) that occupies the exact size until the video loads.

Lighthouse recorded an LCP of 1.9 seconds and a CLS of 0.0 because the skeleton prevents layout shift. The experiment taught me that a tiny placeholder plus deferred source can keep the cinematic feel without sacrificing performance.

What strategies do you use to balance autoplay policies and lazy loading for hero videos in Next.js projects?

#Nextjs #TypeScript #WebPerformance #Frontend

title: Image Upload & Processing Pipeline Using Prisma and Cloud Storage
angle: I detail how we built a secure, Prisma-backed image upload flow that validates files, stores them in cloud storage, and generates thumbnails for fast product pages.
post:
We cut image-upload latency from 1.2 seconds to 180 milliseconds by streaming files straight to Cloudflare R2 with a presigned PUT URL.

Chronos & Steel is a Next.js 16 watch marketplace where sellers add listings that include high-resolution photos. The upload flow had to be secure, cheap, and fast enough for product pages to render instantly.

When a seller selects a file, the API validates the MIME type and size, writes a placeholder record with Prisma, then calls @aws-sdk/client-s3 to create a single-use PUT URL scoped to the bucket and object key. The browser uploads directly to R2, bypassing the app server. A webhook fires on successful upload, the Prisma record is updated with the final URL, and a Cloudflare Worker generates a 300 px thumbnail that is stored alongside the original.

The thumbnail generation finishes in under 300 ms and proved that decoupling upload from processing avoids race conditions and keeps the request path lightweight.

Has anyone run into edge-case issues when mixing presigned URLs with Prisma transactions, especially around retry logic for failed uploads?

#TypeScript #NextJS #Prisma #CloudflareR2
